Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.B: A 5' cap is an mRNA modification, not a protein N-terminal modification.
distractor_rationales.C: Proteins do not base pair with DNA promoters as part of ER targeting.
distractor_rationales.D: Cytochrome c release is related to apoptosis, not secretory protein targeting.

items.stem: A protein has an isoelectric point of 6.2. It is loaded at pH 8.0 onto an anion-exchange resin that binds negatively charged proteins. Which outcome is most likely?

choices.text: The protein will precipitate because pH 8.0 is below its pI.
The protein will bind the resin because it has a net positive charge.
The protein will pass through because proteins have no charge above their pI.
The protein will bind the resin because it has a net negative charge.

items.explanation: At a pH above its isoelectric point, a protein has a net negative charge. An anion-exchange resin binds anions, so the protein is expected to bind and can later be eluted by increasing salt or changing pH. Common miss: Reversing the sign of a protein's net charge above versus below its pI. This correctly relates pH above pI to net negative charge and anion-exchange binding. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.A: pH 8.0 is above, not below, a pI of 6.2.
distractor_rationales.B: A protein is generally net positive below its pI, not above it.
distractor_rationales.C: Proteins have zero net charge at their pI, not at all pH values above the pI.

items.stem: An inhibitor lowers both the apparent Km and apparent Vmax of a Michaelis-Menten enzyme by the same factor. Which mechanism best explains this kinetic pattern?

choices.text: The inhibitor binds only the enzyme-substrate complex.
The inhibitor competes with substrate for the free enzyme active site.
The inhibitor permanently destroys the enzyme's primary structure.
The inhibitor increases substrate diffusion to the active site.

items.explanation: Uncompetitive inhibitors bind only the enzyme-substrate complex. In the simple Michaelis-Menten model, this decreases both apparent Km and apparent Vmax by the same factor. Common miss: Assuming every reversible inhibitor must bind the free enzyme active site. This is the defining binding pattern and kinetic signature of uncompetitive inhibition. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.B: Competitive inhibition increases apparent Km while leaving Vmax unchanged.
distractor_rationales.C: Irreversible destruction would mainly decrease Vmax and would not predict the matched decrease in apparent Km.
distractor_rationales.D: Improved substrate diffusion would not explain a decreased Vmax.

items.stem: A DNA template strand contains the sequence 3'-TAC GGA CTT ACT-5'. What mRNA sequence would be produced from this template region?

choices.text: 5'-UAC GGA CUU ACU-3'
5'-TAC GGA CTT ACT-3'
3'-AUG CCU GAA UGA-5'
5'-AUG CCU GAA UGA-3'

items.explanation: RNA polymerase reads the DNA template strand antiparallel and synthesizes RNA 5' to 3'. The complement of 3'-TAC GGA CTT ACT-5' is 5'-AUG CCU GAA UGA-3'. Common miss: Complementing the bases but writing the product strand in the wrong direction. This is the correct antiparallel RNA complement with uracil replacing thymine. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.A: This is not the correct complement of the provided template.
distractor_rationales.B: This repeats the DNA template and uses thymine rather than uracil.
distractor_rationales.C: This has the correct base complement but is written in the wrong orientation for the mRNA product.

items.stem: A rapidly dividing cell has abundant NADPH but needs more ribose 5-phosphate for nucleotide synthesis. Which metabolic strategy best matches this need?

choices.text: Convert ribose 5-phosphate directly into lactate to regenerate NAD+.
Run the oxidative pentose phosphate pathway repeatedly to maximize CO2 release from glucose carbon 1.
Block all transketolase reactions so that ribose 5-phosphate cannot equilibrate with glycolytic intermediates.
Use nonoxidative pentose phosphate pathway reactions to convert glycolytic intermediates into ribose 5-phosphate.

items.explanation: When a cell needs ribose 5-phosphate more than NADPH, the reversible nonoxidative reactions of the pentose phosphate pathway can convert fructose 6-phosphate and glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate into ribose 5-phosphate without requiring additional oxidative NADPH production. Common miss: Assuming ribose 5-phosphate production must always be coupled to new NADPH production. This directly supplies ribose 5-phosphate from glycolytic intermediates while avoiding excess NADPH production. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.A: Ribose 5-phosphate is used for nucleotide synthesis, not direct lactate fermentation.
distractor_rationales.B: The oxidative phase is useful for NADPH generation and CO2 release, which is not the stated need.
distractor_rationales.C: Blocking transketolase would impair interconversion between pentose phosphates and glycolytic intermediates.

items.stem: Malonate is a structural analog of succinate that inhibits succinate dehydrogenase. Which immediate effect is most likely in isolated mitochondria supplied primarily with succinate?

choices.text: Increased conversion of oxygen to water by Complex IV
Increased proton pumping by Complex II
Direct inhibition of ATP synthase by preventing proton flow through Fo
Reduced electron entry through Complex II and decreased ubiquinone reduction

items.explanation: Succinate dehydrogenase is Complex II. Inhibiting it reduces electron transfer from succinate-derived FADH2 to ubiquinone, decreasing downstream electron flow from this entry point. Common miss: Forgetting that Complex II transfers electrons to ubiquinone but does not pump protons. This correctly identifies succinate dehydrogenase as Complex II and predicts less ubiquinone reduction. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.A: Reduced electron entry through Complex II would tend to decrease, not increase, downstream oxygen reduction.
distractor_rationales.B: Complex II does not pump protons, and inhibition would not increase its activity.
distractor_rationales.C: Malonate targets succinate dehydrogenase, not ATP synthase.

items.stem: A buried Asp-Lys salt bridge stabilizes a protein's tertiary structure. Replacing the lysine with leucine is most likely to have which effect?

choices.text: Destabilization caused by loss of a favorable ionic interaction
Stabilization caused by creation of a new disulfide bond
No effect because lysine and leucine are both positively charged
Conversion of the protein backbone into a nucleic acid backbone

items.explanation: Lysine is positively charged at physiological pH and can form a salt bridge with negatively charged aspartate. Leucine is nonpolar and cannot maintain that ionic interaction, so the tertiary structure may be destabilized. Common miss: Classifying leucine as basic because it is sometimes grouped with hydrophobic residues in protein interiors. This correctly identifies the lost salt bridge as the main predicted effect. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.B: Leucine does not form disulfide bonds; cysteine residues do.
distractor_rationales.C: Leucine is nonpolar, not positively charged.
distractor_rationales.D: An amino acid substitution does not alter the chemical identity of the protein backbone.

items.stem: Two double-stranded DNA fragments have the same length. Fragment 1 is 70% GC, whereas Fragment 2 is 30% GC. Which comparison is most likely?

choices.text: Fragment 1 cannot form a double helix because GC pairs are not complementary.
Fragment 2 has a higher melting temperature because AT pairs contain more hydrogen bonds.
Both fragments must have identical melting temperatures because length alone determines DNA stability.
Fragment 1 has a higher melting temperature because GC-rich DNA is generally more thermally stable.

items.explanation: GC-rich DNA typically melts at a higher temperature because GC base pairs have three hydrogen bonds and favorable stacking interactions relative to AT-rich DNA of the same length. Common miss: Overlooking base composition and treating all same-length DNA duplexes as equally stable. This correctly predicts higher thermal stability for the GC-rich fragment. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.A: G and C are complementary Watson-Crick partners.
distractor_rationales.B: AT pairs have two hydrogen bonds, not more than GC pairs.
distractor_rationales.C: Length matters, but base composition also affects melting temperature.

items.stem: An enzyme has a Hill coefficient of 0.6 for its substrate. Which interpretation is most consistent with this value?

choices.text: Binding of substrate to one site increases substrate affinity at other sites.
Binding of substrate to one site decreases substrate affinity at other sites.
The enzyme is inactive because Hill coefficients below 1 are impossible.
The enzyme has exactly 0.6 active sites per molecule.

items.explanation: A Hill coefficient less than 1 indicates negative cooperativity, meaning substrate binding at one site lowers the apparent affinity of other binding sites. It does not directly equal the number of active sites. Common miss: Treating the Hill coefficient as a literal count of active sites. This correctly describes negative cooperativity. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.A: This describes positive cooperativity, which corresponds to a Hill coefficient greater than 1.
distractor_rationales.C: Hill coefficients below 1 can occur and are interpreted as negative cooperativity.
distractor_rationales.D: The Hill coefficient is not simply the number of active sites.

items.stem: In a model plant, loss of enzyme Q is caused by a completely recessive allele q. Two heterozygous plants are crossed. Among offspring that have normal enzyme Q activity, what fraction are expected to be carriers?
items.explanation: A Qq x Qq cross produces genotypes 1 QQ : 2 Qq : 1 qq. Among offspring with normal enzyme activity, qq is excluded, leaving 1 QQ and 2 Qq. Therefore, 2 of the 3 normal-activity offspring are carriers. Common miss: Using the carrier fraction among all offspring rather than conditioning on normal phenotype. This correctly applies conditional probability after excluding recessive-loss offspring. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.A: This is the fraction of all offspring expected to be qq, not the carrier fraction among normal offspring.
distractor_rationales.B: This is the fraction of normal offspring expected to be QQ.
distractor_rationales.C: This is the carrier fraction among all offspring, not conditional on normal activity.

items.stem: Oxidation of FADH2 generally yields less ATP than oxidation of NADH in mitochondria. Which explanation best accounts for this difference?

choices.text: FADH2 oxidation consumes the proton gradient rather than contributing to it.
FADH2 donates electrons directly to ATP synthase.
NADH is oxidized only in the cytosol and never donates electrons to mitochondria.
FADH2-derived electrons enter at Complex II and bypass proton pumping at Complex I.

items.explanation: NADH donates electrons through Complex I, which pumps protons. FADH2-derived electrons often enter through Complex II, which does not pump protons, so fewer protons are moved per electron pair and less ATP is generated. Common miss: Thinking ATP yield depends only on electron number rather than the entry point into the electron transport chain. This correctly identifies the bypass of Complex I proton pumping. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.A: FADH2 oxidation supports electron transport; it does not directly consume the proton gradient.
distractor_rationales.B: ATP synthase uses proton flow and does not directly accept electrons from FADH2.
distractor_rationales.C: Mitochondrial NADH donates electrons to Complex I.

items.stem: During oxidation of lactate to pyruvate, NAD+ is converted to NADH. Which statement best describes the role of NAD+ in this reaction?

choices.text: NAD+ forms a peptide bond with pyruvate.
NAD+ is oxidized by donating electrons to lactate.
NAD+ is reduced by accepting electrons as a hydride equivalent.
NAD+ is converted into ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation.

items.explanation: When lactate is oxidized to pyruvate, NAD+ accepts reducing equivalents and becomes NADH. Gain of electrons is reduction. Common miss: Mixing up oxidation and reduction from the perspective of the cofactor. This correctly describes NAD+ as the electron acceptor that is reduced to NADH. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.A: NAD+ does not form peptide bonds with pyruvate.
distractor_rationales.B: NAD+ is reduced, not oxidized, in this reaction.
distractor_rationales.D: NADH formation is a redox event, not substrate-level phosphorylation.

items.stem: Which molecule is a nucleotide rather than a nucleoside?

choices.text: Guanosine
Adenosine
Adenosine monophosphate
Cytidine

items.explanation: A nucleotide contains a nitrogenous base, a sugar, and at least one phosphate group. Adenosine monophosphate contains adenine, ribose, and phosphate, whereas adenosine, guanosine, and cytidine are nucleosides without phosphate in their names. Common miss: Using the base identity rather than the presence of phosphate to distinguish nucleotides from nucleosides. This contains a phosphate group and is therefore a nucleotide. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.A: Guanosine is a nucleoside composed of guanine plus ribose.
distractor_rationales.B: Adenosine is a nucleoside composed of adenine plus ribose.
distractor_rationales.D: Cytidine is a nucleoside composed of cytosine plus ribose.

items.stem: A covalent inhibitor modifies an essential active-site residue in 30% of enzyme molecules. After excess inhibitor is removed by dialysis, activity remains 70% of the original value. Which kinetic effect is most likely when substrate is varied?

choices.text: The enzyme becomes positively cooperative even if it was monomeric.
Km increases, while Vmax remains unchanged.
Both Km and Vmax increase because dialysis activates the enzyme.
Vmax decreases, while the Km of the remaining active enzyme is largely unchanged.

items.explanation: Irreversible inactivation reduces the concentration of active enzyme molecules. This lowers Vmax, which depends on active enzyme concentration, while the substrate affinity of the remaining unmodified enzyme molecules can remain approximately the same. Common miss: Treating irreversible inhibition as though it must change substrate affinity of the remaining active enzyme. This is the expected effect of reducing active enzyme concentration. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.A: Irreversible modification does not by itself create cooperativity in a monomeric enzyme.
distractor_rationales.B: This pattern is typical of competitive inhibition, not irreversible loss of enzyme molecules.
distractor_rationales.C: Dialysis removes free inhibitor but does not reverse covalent modification in the stem.

items.stem: A mutation reduces the activity of phosphoglycerate kinase in glycolysis. Which direct consequence is most likely?

choices.text: Direct oxidation of pyruvate to CO2 in the cytosol
Increased production of ribose 5-phosphate by ATP synthase
Reduced ATP formation from 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate
Replacement of NAD+ with FAD as the glycolytic electron acceptor

items.explanation: Phosphoglycerate kinase catalyzes a substrate-level phosphorylation step in which 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate transfers a phosphoryl group to ADP to form ATP and 3-phosphoglycerate. Common miss: Confusing substrate-level phosphorylation in glycolysis with ATP synthesis by oxidative phosphorylation. This is the direct reaction catalyzed by phosphoglycerate kinase. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.A: Complete oxidation of pyruvate to CO2 does not occur directly in the cytosol.
distractor_rationales.B: ATP synthase is part of oxidative phosphorylation, not ribose 5-phosphate production.
distractor_rationales.D: Glycolysis uses NAD+ at the glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate dehydrogenase step, not FAD as a replacement.

items.stem: A mutation disrupts the TATA box of a eukaryotic protein-coding gene. Which process is most directly affected?

choices.text: Base pairing between codons and anticodons during elongation
Hydrolysis of mischarged tRNA in the ribosomal A site
Recruitment of general transcription factors and RNA polymerase II
Proton pumping by Complex IV

items.explanation: The TATA box is a promoter element that helps position the transcription initiation machinery for many eukaryotic protein-coding genes. Disrupting it most directly impairs transcription initiation by RNA polymerase II. Common miss: Confusing promoter mutations with mutations in the translated coding sequence. This correctly identifies the promoter-level effect. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.A: Codon-anticodon pairing occurs during translation, not promoter recognition.
distractor_rationales.B: tRNA editing is a translation fidelity process and is unrelated to a TATA-box mutation.
distractor_rationales.D: Complex IV is part of oxidative phosphorylation, not transcription initiation.

items.stem: Which feature most directly explains why peptide bonds are planar and have restricted rotation?

choices.text: Peptide bonds are phosphodiester bonds between amino acids.
Resonance gives the peptide bond partial double-bond character.
Every peptide bond contains a disulfide linkage.
Peptide bonds are held together only by hydrogen bonds.

items.explanation: The peptide bond has resonance between the carbonyl carbon, carbonyl oxygen, and amide nitrogen. This gives the C-N bond partial double-bond character, making it planar and restricting rotation. Common miss: Confusing covalent peptide bond structure with noncovalent interactions that stabilize secondary structure. This correctly explains peptide bond planarity. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.A: Phosphodiester bonds are found in nucleic acid backbones, not between amino acids in proteins.
distractor_rationales.C: Disulfide linkages occur between cysteine side chains, not in every peptide bond.
distractor_rationales.D: Peptide bonds are covalent amide bonds, not merely hydrogen bonds.

items.stem: A single nucleotide is inserted near the beginning of a coding sequence, and the insertion is not a multiple of three nucleotides. Which outcome is most likely?

choices.text: Improved ribosome proofreading of the original mRNA sequence
A silent mutation because insertions never affect codon reading frame
A substitution of exactly one amino acid with no downstream effect
A frameshift that changes downstream codons and may introduce a premature stop codon

items.explanation: Insertions or deletions that are not multiples of three shift the reading frame. A frameshift near the start of a coding sequence changes many downstream codons and can produce an early stop codon. Common miss: Treating a one-base insertion like a one-base substitution. This correctly describes the likely consequence of a non-triplet insertion. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.A: Ribosome proofreading would not restore the original mRNA sequence.
distractor_rationales.B: Insertions can strongly affect the reading frame.
distractor_rationales.C: A single amino acid substitution is more typical of a missense point mutation, not a frameshift insertion.

items.stem: In liver cells, pyruvate kinase is inhibited by high ATP and activated by fructose 1,6-bisphosphate. Which interpretation best explains this regulation?

choices.text: Fructose 1,6-bisphosphate is the direct product of pyruvate kinase.
High ATP indicates that glycolysis must accelerate regardless of substrate availability.
High ATP signals sufficient energy, while fructose 1,6-bisphosphate provides feed-forward activation when glycolytic flux is high.
Pyruvate kinase is a mitochondrial electron transport complex.

items.explanation: Pyruvate kinase catalyzes a late glycolytic step. ATP inhibition helps slow glycolysis when energy is abundant, whereas fructose 1,6-bisphosphate indicates upstream glycolytic commitment and activates the downstream step. Common miss: Interpreting ATP as a substrate-like activator for all metabolic enzymes. This correctly connects energy status and feed-forward regulation. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.A: Fructose 1,6-bisphosphate is produced upstream of pyruvate kinase, not by pyruvate kinase.
distractor_rationales.B: High ATP usually inhibits energy-producing catabolic pathways.
distractor_rationales.D: Pyruvate kinase is a cytosolic glycolytic enzyme, not an electron transport complex.

items.stem: During DNA synthesis, a polymerase adds a new nucleotide to which chemical group on the growing strand?

choices.text: The amino terminus of the first nucleotide
The methyl group of thymine
The free 3' hydroxyl group
The peptide bond of the previous nucleotide

items.explanation: DNA polymerases extend nucleic acid strands by adding incoming nucleotides to the free 3' hydroxyl of the growing strand, forming a phosphodiester bond and synthesizing in the 5' to 3' direction. Common miss: Remembering strand directionality but not the chemical group that is extended. This correctly identifies the reactive group on the growing strand. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.A: Nucleotides do not have amino termini analogous to proteins.
distractor_rationales.B: The thymine methyl group is not used to extend DNA.
distractor_rationales.D: Nucleotides are joined by phosphodiester bonds, not peptide bonds.

items.stem: In mitochondria, the intermembrane space is more acidic than the matrix during active respiration. Which movement is directly coupled to ATP synthesis by ATP synthase?

choices.text: Protons moving from the intermembrane space into the matrix
Protons moving from the matrix into the intermembrane space through ATP synthase
Electrons moving through the Fo subunit into the matrix
Glucose moving through Complex IV into the intermembrane space

items.explanation: The electron transport chain pumps protons from the matrix to the intermembrane space. ATP synthase uses the downhill return of protons into the matrix to drive ATP formation. Common miss: Confusing the direction of respiratory proton pumping with the direction of proton flow through ATP synthase. This is the proton flow used by ATP synthase during ATP production. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.B: This is the direction of proton pumping by the electron transport chain, not ATP-producing flow through ATP synthase.
distractor_rationales.C: ATP synthase conducts protons, not electrons.
distractor_rationales.D: Glucose does not move through Complex IV.

items.stem: A researcher wants to replace a surface-exposed glutamate with a residue that preserves negative charge at physiological pH but changes side-chain length. Which substitution best fits this goal?

choices.text: Lysine
Aspartate
Phenylalanine
Asparagine

items.explanation: Glutamate and aspartate are both negatively charged acidic amino acids at physiological pH, but aspartate has a shorter side chain. This makes Asp the best substitution for preserving charge while changing length. Common miss: Choosing an amide residue because its name resembles an acidic residue, despite loss of charge. This preserves negative charge while shortening the side chain. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.A: Lysine is positively charged at physiological pH.
distractor_rationales.C: Phenylalanine is bulky and hydrophobic rather than negatively charged.
distractor_rationales.D: Asparagine is polar but uncharged at physiological pH.

items.stem: A mature eukaryotic mRNA is found in the cytosol with a 5' cap and poly(A) tail but contains no introns. Which process most directly removed the introns?

choices.text: Splicing of the pre-mRNA by spliceosomal machinery
Peptide bond formation by the ribosome
Replication of the DNA template by DNA polymerase
Oxidation of NADH by the electron transport chain

items.explanation: Eukaryotic pre-mRNAs commonly undergo splicing, in which introns are removed and exons are joined. The 5' cap and poly(A) tail are separate mRNA processing features. Common miss: Grouping all mRNA processing events together without distinguishing splicing from capping and polyadenylation. This correctly identifies intron removal as splicing. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.B: Ribosomes translate mature mRNA but do not remove introns.
distractor_rationales.C: DNA replication copies DNA and does not process mRNA.
distractor_rationales.D: NADH oxidation is metabolic and unrelated to intron removal.

items.stem: An enzyme-catalyzed reaction has a negative Delta G under cellular conditions. What does this imply about the enzyme's effect on the reaction?

choices.text: The reaction is thermodynamically favorable, and the enzyme accelerates approach to equilibrium without changing Delta G.
The enzyme makes the reaction favorable by lowering the free energy of products only.
The enzyme changes the equilibrium constant so that only products can exist.
The reaction cannot occur because all enzyme-catalyzed reactions require positive Delta G.

items.explanation: A negative Delta G means the reaction is thermodynamically favorable as written under the specified conditions. Enzymes lower activation energy and increase reaction rate, but they do not change Delta G or the equilibrium constant. Common miss: Thinking enzymes change reaction free energy rather than activation energy. This correctly separates thermodynamics from catalysis. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.B: Enzymes do not make reactions favorable by selectively lowering product free energy.
distractor_rationales.C: Enzymes do not alter the equilibrium constant.
distractor_rationales.D: Many enzyme-catalyzed reactions have negative Delta G under cellular conditions.

items.stem: A heterozygous Aa organism is crossed with an aa organism. If A is completely dominant to a and the locus does not affect viability, what phenotype ratio is expected among offspring?

choices.text: All dominant phenotype
3 dominant phenotype : 1 recessive phenotype
9 dominant phenotype : 7 recessive phenotype
1 dominant phenotype : 1 recessive phenotype

items.explanation: The Aa parent produces A and a gametes in equal proportions, while the aa parent produces only a gametes. The offspring are 1 Aa and 1 aa, giving a 1:1 phenotype ratio. Common miss: Using the heterozygote self-cross ratio instead of the testcross ratio. This is the expected result of a single-locus testcross. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.A: Half the offspring are expected to be aa and show the recessive phenotype.
distractor_rationales.B: A 3:1 ratio is expected from selfing two heterozygotes at one locus.
distractor_rationales.C: A 9:7 ratio is a two-gene complementary interaction pattern, not this single-locus cross.

items.stem: A mitochondrial preparation is supplied with ADP and phosphate, but the inner mitochondrial membrane is mechanically ruptured. Which outcome is most likely?

choices.text: Electron transfer becomes unnecessary because ADP donates electrons directly to oxygen.
ATP synthesis increases because protons can diffuse freely to ATP synthase.
ATP synthesis decreases because the proton gradient cannot be maintained.
The mitochondrial DNA code changes to compensate for membrane rupture.

items.explanation: Oxidative phosphorylation requires an intact inner mitochondrial membrane to maintain the proton-motive force. If the membrane is ruptured, protons cannot be compartmentalized effectively, so ATP synthesis by ATP synthase decreases. Common miss: Thinking proton access alone is sufficient for ATP synthesis, rather than recognizing the need for a gradient. This correctly identifies loss of the proton gradient as the key consequence. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.A: ADP does not donate electrons to oxygen in the electron transport chain.
distractor_rationales.B: Free proton diffusion dissipates the gradient rather than improving ATP synthesis.
distractor_rationales.D: Membrane damage does not alter the genetic code.

items.stem: A participant can detect a dim light on 50% of trials when it is presented in a dark room. In psychophysics, this light intensity is best described as the participant's:

choices.text: Difference threshold
Absolute threshold
Sensory adaptation point
Signal detection criterion

items.explanation: An absolute threshold is the minimum stimulus intensity detected 50% of the time under specified conditions. The stem describes detection of a single faint stimulus, not detection of a change between two stimuli or a decision bias. Common miss: Confusing the absolute threshold for detecting a stimulus with the difference threshold for detecting a change between stimuli. This is correct. Detecting a stimulus on 50% of trials defines the absolute threshold in a typical psychophysical task. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.A: A difference threshold is the smallest detectable difference between two stimulus intensities, not the minimum detectable intensity of one stimulus.
distractor_rationales.C: Sensory adaptation refers to reduced responsiveness after repeated or sustained stimulation, which is not the focus of the stem.
distractor_rationales.D: A signal detection criterion is the decision rule used to say a stimulus is present; it is related but not the threshold described here.

items.stem: A student studies Spanish vocabulary in the same quiet library room each day. On test day, the student notices that recalling the words feels easier when sitting in that same room than when sitting in a noisy cafeteria. Which memory principle best explains this observation?

choices.text: Context-dependent retrieval
Proactive interference
Procedural memory
Source monitoring error

items.explanation: Context-dependent retrieval occurs when memory is improved because the retrieval context overlaps with the encoding context. The same physical environment can serve as a retrieval cue for information learned there. Common miss: Treating any improvement in memory as simple rehearsal rather than identifying the role of environmental retrieval cues. This is correct. The library context present during encoding also aids retrieval. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.B: Proactive interference occurs when older learning disrupts newer learning; the stem does not describe interference from previously learned material.
distractor_rationales.C: Procedural memory concerns skills and habits, not recall of vocabulary words in a matching environment.
distractor_rationales.D: A source monitoring error involves misattributing where information came from, which is not described.

items.stem: A researcher studying decision-making finds that participants estimate shark attacks as more common than diabetes-related deaths after watching a dramatic documentary about shark attacks. Which cognitive heuristic most directly explains this judgment?

choices.text: Representativeness heuristic
Availability heuristic
Algorithmic reasoning
Conservation error

items.explanation: The availability heuristic occurs when people estimate likelihood based on how easily examples come to mind. The documentary made shark attacks more mentally accessible, biasing frequency judgments. Common miss: Confusing availability, which depends on ease of recall, with representativeness, which depends on perceived similarity. This is correct. Recently vivid examples are more available in memory and can inflate perceived frequency. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.A: The representativeness heuristic involves judging category membership by similarity to a prototype, not by ease of recall.
distractor_rationales.C: Algorithmic reasoning refers to systematic step-by-step problem solving, which would reduce rather than explain this bias.
distractor_rationales.D: A conservation error is associated with cognitive development tasks, not adult probability estimation after vivid exposure.

items.stem: A patient in a fictional educational case has damage to the hippocampus after a laboratory accident. Which outcome would be most expected?

choices.text: Complete loss of autonomic regulation
Loss of all spinal reflexes
Inability to detect light intensity
Impaired formation of new explicit memories

items.explanation: The hippocampus is important for forming new explicit, declarative memories. Damage often produces difficulty encoding new facts and events, while many reflexive and sensory functions remain mediated by other structures. Common miss: Overgeneralizing brain damage as causing broad impairment rather than linking the hippocampus specifically to declarative memory formation. This is correct. The hippocampus supports consolidation of new explicit memories. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.A: Autonomic regulation involves hypothalamic, brainstem, and peripheral mechanisms more directly than the hippocampus.
distractor_rationales.B: Spinal reflexes are mediated by spinal circuits and do not depend on the hippocampus.
distractor_rationales.C: Light detection begins with retinal photoreceptors and visual pathways, not the hippocampus.

items.stem: A child receives a small sticker each time she completes her reading homework. After collecting ten stickers, she can trade them for extra playtime. This arrangement is best described as:

choices.text: Classical conditioning using an unconditioned stimulus
Operant conditioning using a token economy
Negative punishment using extinction
Latent learning without reinforcement

items.explanation: The stickers function as tokens earned after a desired behavior and later exchanged for a reinforcer. This is an operant conditioning arrangement because consequences are used to increase homework completion. Common miss: Mislabeling any learned association as classical conditioning even when the behavior is shaped by consequences. This is correct. Stickers are tokens that can be exchanged for a backup reinforcer. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.A: Classical conditioning pairs stimuli to elicit reflexive responses; the stem involves consequences following voluntary behavior.
distractor_rationales.C: Negative punishment removes a desirable stimulus to reduce behavior, whereas the child gains stickers to increase behavior.
distractor_rationales.D: Latent learning occurs without obvious reinforcement, but the stem explicitly uses reinforcement.

items.stem: A worker feels anxious whenever a supervisor walks by because the supervisor often assigns extra tasks without warning. After several weeks in which the supervisor walks by without assigning extra tasks, the worker's anxiety gradually decreases. Which learning process is most directly illustrated by the decrease in anxiety?

choices.text: Stimulus generalization
Extinction
Positive punishment
Observational learning

items.explanation: Extinction in classical conditioning occurs when a conditioned stimulus is repeatedly presented without the unconditioned stimulus, reducing the conditioned response. The supervisor walking by no longer predicts extra tasks, so anxiety decreases. Common miss: Mistaking a reduced conditioned emotional response for punishment rather than extinction. This is correct. The predictive cue is repeatedly presented without the expected outcome. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.A: Stimulus generalization would involve similar cues also producing anxiety, which is not the main process described.
distractor_rationales.C: Positive punishment adds an unpleasant consequence to reduce behavior, but the stem describes a conditioned emotional response decreasing.
distractor_rationales.D: Observational learning involves learning by watching others, which is not described.

items.stem: A sociologist argues that schools reproduce inequality by rewarding cultural knowledge and interaction styles that are more common among higher-income families. This argument most closely reflects which concept?

choices.text: Role strain
Cultural capital
Primary deviance
Social facilitation

items.explanation: Cultural capital refers to nonfinancial social assets, such as language styles, tastes, knowledge, and dispositions, that can provide advantages in institutional settings. The scenario focuses on how schools reward class-linked cultural resources. Common miss: Reducing social class to income alone and missing the role of nonfinancial resources in institutional advantage. This is correct. The argument concerns unequal rewards for class-linked cultural knowledge and interaction styles. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.A: Role strain involves tension within a single social role, not institutional reproduction of inequality.
distractor_rationales.C: Primary deviance refers to initial norm violation before deviant identity is internalized, which is unrelated to the school reward system described.
distractor_rationales.D: Social facilitation is improved performance in the presence of others on simple or well-learned tasks.

items.stem: In a fictional survey, adults reporting chronic job insecurity also report frequent headaches and sleep difficulty. Which biological pathway most directly links chronic stress to these physical outcomes?

choices.text: Inactivation of all sympathetic nervous system responses
Activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis and sustained glucocorticoid release
Permanent loss of sensory receptor transduction
Immediate elimination of negative feedback in the pancreas

items.explanation: Chronic stress can activate the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, increasing glucocorticoid exposure and affecting sleep, immune function, and other physiological systems. The other choices describe overly broad or unrelated mechanisms. Common miss: Treating stress as purely psychological rather than recognizing neuroendocrine mechanisms. This is correct. The HPA axis is a central biological pathway in stress physiology. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.A: Stress generally activates, rather than inactivates, sympathetic responses.
distractor_rationales.C: Stress does not require permanent loss of sensory transduction to cause headaches or sleep difficulty.
distractor_rationales.D: The pancreas is not the primary pathway linking psychosocial stress to the outcomes described.

items.stem: An adolescent explores several religious, occupational, and political possibilities but has not yet made stable commitments. According to Marcia's identity status framework, this adolescent is best described as being in:

choices.text: Identity diffusion
Identity foreclosure
Identity moratorium
Identity achievement

items.explanation: Identity moratorium involves active exploration without firm commitment. The adolescent is considering alternatives but has not yet settled on stable commitments. Common miss: Confusing moratorium with diffusion because both involve lack of final commitment, while only moratorium involves active exploration. This is correct. The adolescent is exploring options but has not committed. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.A: Identity diffusion involves neither active exploration nor commitment.
distractor_rationales.B: Identity foreclosure involves commitment without sufficient exploration, often adopting others' expectations.
distractor_rationales.D: Identity achievement involves commitment after exploration.

items.stem: A researcher wants to measure whether participants can detect a faint tone while accounting separately for sensory sensitivity and willingness to say, "I heard it." Which framework is most appropriate?

choices.text: Signal detection theory
Social constructionism
Drive reduction theory
Cognitive dissonance theory

items.explanation: Signal detection theory distinguishes actual sensitivity from response criterion. It is useful when hits, misses, false alarms, and correct rejections are affected by both sensory ability and decision bias. Common miss: Using absolute threshold alone when the study specifically asks to separate sensitivity from decision criterion. This is correct. Signal detection theory separates sensitivity from response bias. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.B: Social constructionism concerns how meanings and categories are created through social processes, not sensory decision thresholds.
distractor_rationales.C: Drive reduction theory concerns motivation to reduce physiological needs, not detection judgments.
distractor_rationales.D: Cognitive dissonance theory concerns discomfort from inconsistent beliefs or behaviors.

items.stem: A child understands that the amount of water remains the same when it is poured from a short wide glass into a tall narrow glass. In Piaget's theory, this understanding is called:

choices.text: Object permanence
Conservation
Egocentrism
Formal operational reasoning

items.explanation: Conservation is the understanding that quantity remains the same despite changes in shape or appearance. The water task is a classic example of conservation of liquid volume. Common miss: Confusing concrete operational conservation with formal operational abstract reasoning. This is correct. The child recognizes that volume is conserved across container shape changes. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.A: Object permanence is the understanding that objects continue to exist when out of sight.
distractor_rationales.C: Egocentrism is difficulty taking another person's perspective, not understanding volume constancy.
distractor_rationales.D: Formal operational reasoning involves abstract and hypothetical reasoning, which is broader than the conservation judgment described.

items.stem: A fictional client reports persistent low mood, loss of interest in usual activities, disrupted sleep, and feelings of worthlessness for several weeks. For MCAT-level classification, this pattern is most consistent with symptoms of:

choices.text: Dissociative identity disorder
Specific phobia
Major depressive disorder
Antisocial personality disorder

items.explanation: The symptom cluster of sustained low mood, anhedonia, sleep disruption, and worthlessness is characteristic of depressive disorders, especially major depressive disorder in broad MCAT-level classification. This is an educational classification, not a diagnosis. Common miss: Focusing on one symptom such as sleep disruption rather than the overall depressive symptom pattern. This is correct. The pattern aligns most closely with depressive symptoms. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.A: Dissociative identity disorder involves distinct identity states and memory disruption, which are not described.
distractor_rationales.B: Specific phobia centers on intense fear of a specific object or situation, not persistent low mood and anhedonia.
distractor_rationales.D: Antisocial personality disorder involves pervasive disregard for others' rights and social norms, which is not described.

items.stem: A researcher finds that participants from lower-income neighborhoods report higher exposure to environmental noise and higher perceived stress. The researcher concludes that low income directly causes stress. Which critique is most appropriate?

choices.text: The conclusion may be too strong because the observational design cannot rule out confounding variables.
The conclusion is invalid because stress cannot be measured by self-report.
The conclusion is certain because income is a biological variable.
The conclusion is invalid because neighborhood noise is unrelated to stress responses.

items.explanation: An observational association does not by itself establish direct causation. Other variables, such as housing quality, work demands, discrimination, health status, or safety concerns, could contribute to the relationship. Common miss: Treating correlation as causation because the proposed causal pathway is plausible. This is correct. The causal claim exceeds what the observational design can establish. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.B: Self-report can be a valid measurement method, though it has limitations.
distractor_rationales.C: Income is socioeconomic rather than biological, and an association alone does not prove causation.
distractor_rationales.D: Noise exposure can plausibly relate to stress, so the issue is causal inference rather than impossibility.

items.stem: A student hears a loud crash and immediately experiences increased heart rate and sweating. A few seconds later, the student identifies the sound as a dropped metal tray and begins to calm down. Which nervous system division most directly produced the immediate increase in heart rate and sweating?

choices.text: Somatic motor division controlling skeletal muscles only
Parasympathetic division of the autonomic nervous system
Sympathetic division of the autonomic nervous system
Enteric nervous system controlling digestion only

items.explanation: The sympathetic division supports fight-or-flight responses, including increased heart rate and sweating. Calming after reappraisal involves reduced sympathetic activation and increased parasympathetic influence. Common miss: Attributing all rapid bodily responses to voluntary somatic control rather than autonomic sympathetic activation. This is correct. Sympathetic activation produces the immediate arousal response. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.A: The somatic motor division controls voluntary skeletal muscle movement, not sweating and heart rate directly.
distractor_rationales.B: Parasympathetic activity generally supports rest-and-digest functions and slowing of heart rate.
distractor_rationales.D: The enteric nervous system regulates gastrointestinal functions and is not the direct source of the described arousal response.

items.stem: A sociologist studies brief face-to-face interactions between bus drivers and passengers to understand how politeness rituals maintain a sense of social order. This focus is most characteristic of:

choices.text: Demographic transition theory
World-systems theory
Microsociology
Structural mobility analysis only

items.explanation: Microsociology focuses on small-scale social interactions and meanings in everyday life. Studying politeness rituals in brief interpersonal encounters fits this level of analysis. Common miss: Assuming all sociology focuses on large institutions and missing the microlevel interaction focus. This is correct. The study examines small-scale interactions. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.A: Demographic transition theory concerns population changes associated with industrialization and development.
distractor_rationales.B: World-systems theory examines global economic relationships among countries or regions.
distractor_rationales.D: Structural mobility concerns movement caused by changes in the social hierarchy, not microlevel interaction rituals.

items.stem: A participant in a reaction-time study responds faster when a warning light reliably appears 500 ms before the target than when no warning light appears. The warning light most likely improves performance by:

choices.text: Preventing the target from entering sensory memory
Increasing the absolute threshold for detecting the target
Eliminating all sensory adaptation
Serving as a cue that helps orient attention before the target appears

items.explanation: A reliable warning cue can orient attention and prepare a response, reducing reaction time. It does not improve performance by raising the detection threshold or preventing sensory encoding. Common miss: Misinterpreting a beneficial attentional cue as a change in sensory threshold. This is correct. A predictive cue can improve attentional readiness. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.A: Preventing sensory memory would impair detection, not improve reaction time.
distractor_rationales.B: Increasing an absolute threshold would make detection harder, not faster.
distractor_rationales.C: The stem does not involve sustained stimulation or adaptation.

items.stem: A fictional study finds that people who repeatedly avoid elevators after one frightening elevator incident feel temporary relief each time they take the stairs. Over time, their elevator fear persists. The persistence of avoidance is best explained by:

choices.text: Habituation
Positive punishment
Negative reinforcement
Latent inhibition

items.explanation: Avoidance is strengthened because it removes or reduces anxiety, which is an aversive state. This is negative reinforcement because behavior increases when something unpleasant is removed. Common miss: Thinking negative reinforcement means punishment because the word negative is used. This is correct. Taking the stairs is reinforced by relief from anxiety. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.A: Habituation would involve reduced response after repeated exposure; avoidance prevents such exposure.
distractor_rationales.B: Positive punishment would add an unpleasant consequence to decrease behavior, which is not described.
distractor_rationales.D: Latent inhibition refers to slower conditioning to a familiar stimulus, not maintenance of avoidance through relief.

items.stem: In a fictional experiment, participants memorize a list of words and then immediately learn a second list of similar words. Later, memory for the first list is worse than it would have been without the second list. This effect is best described as:

choices.text: Proactive interference
Retroactive interference
Iconic memory
Priming

items.explanation: Retroactive interference occurs when newly learned information interferes with retrieval of previously learned information. The second list reduces later memory for the first list. Common miss: Reversing proactive and retroactive interference. This is correct. New learning interferes with old learning. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.A: Proactive interference occurs when old learning interferes with new learning, the reverse direction.
distractor_rationales.C: Iconic memory is brief visual sensory memory and does not explain list interference.
distractor_rationales.D: Priming is facilitated processing due to prior exposure, not impaired recall due to similar later material.

items.stem: Which research question is most aligned with a symbolic interactionist approach?

choices.text: How do national income distributions predict mortality across countries?
How do patients and clinicians negotiate the meaning of the label "noncompliant" during clinical conversations?
How does cortisol bind to intracellular receptors after stress exposure?
How does random assignment reduce selection bias in experiments?

items.explanation: Symbolic interactionism focuses on how people create, interpret, and negotiate meaning through social interaction. The meaning of a label in clinician-patient interaction is a strong fit. Common miss: Associating symbolic interactionism with any social topic, rather than specifically with interaction-based meaning-making. This is correct. It examines meaning-making in interaction. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.A: This is a macrosociological question about population-level inequality and health.
distractor_rationales.C: This is a biological question about hormone signaling, not social meaning.
distractor_rationales.D: This is a methods question about study design rather than symbolic interaction.

items.stem: A fictional patient has trouble recognizing emotional facial expressions after damage to a medial temporal lobe structure involved in threat processing. Which structure is most likely affected?

choices.text: Amygdala
Cerebellum
Primary motor cortex
Broca's area

items.explanation: The amygdala is involved in emotional processing, especially threat and fear-related learning, and is located in the medial temporal lobe. Damage can affect recognition of emotional facial expressions. Common miss: Choosing hippocampus-like memory structures generally rather than the amygdala's specific role in emotional threat processing. This is correct. The amygdala is the medial temporal structure most linked to threat and emotional expression processing. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.B: The cerebellum is primarily associated with coordination and motor learning, not the described emotional recognition deficit.
distractor_rationales.C: Primary motor cortex controls voluntary movement rather than threat-related facial emotion recognition.
distractor_rationales.D: Broca's area is involved in speech production, not primarily emotional facial expression recognition.

items.stem: A student evaluates a study showing that a new mindfulness app is associated with lower stress among users. Users chose whether to download the app. Which improvement would best address selection bias?

choices.text: Advertise the study using brighter colors.
Randomly assign interested participants to app access or a comparison condition.
Measure stress only after app users have completed the program.
Exclude all participants who report high baseline stress.

items.explanation: Selection bias is likely if app users differ systematically from nonusers before the intervention. Random assignment to app access or comparison condition helps create more equivalent groups. Common miss: Assuming a larger or more attractive recruitment effort eliminates systematic differences between self-selected users and nonusers. This is correct. Random assignment directly addresses preexisting group differences. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.A: Advertising design does not address whether app users differ from nonusers.
distractor_rationales.C: Measuring only after app use prevents evaluating baseline differences and change over time.
distractor_rationales.D: Excluding high-stress participants reduces generalizability and does not solve selection bias among remaining participants.

items.stem: A person remembers how to ride a bicycle after many years without practice but cannot recall the name of the person who taught them. The preserved bicycle skill is primarily an example of:

choices.text: Semantic memory
Episodic memory
Procedural memory
Echoic memory

items.explanation: Procedural memory stores skills and habits, such as riding a bicycle. Remembering the teacher's name would involve declarative memory rather than the motor skill itself. Common miss: Classifying all long-lasting memories as declarative memories rather than distinguishing skill memory from factual or episodic memory. This is correct. Bicycle riding is a learned motor skill. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.A: Semantic memory concerns facts and general knowledge, not a motor skill.
distractor_rationales.B: Episodic memory concerns personal events and experiences, such as a specific lesson.
distractor_rationales.D: Echoic memory is brief auditory sensory memory.

items.stem: A fictional brain-imaging study finds increased activity in the prefrontal cortex while participants suppress an automatic but incorrect response on a Stroop-like task. This finding most directly relates to:

choices.text: Executive control
Phototransduction
Spinal reflex integration
Primary auditory transduction

items.explanation: The prefrontal cortex is strongly involved in executive functions such as inhibitory control, working memory, and flexible rule use. Suppressing an automatic incorrect response on a Stroop-like task requires executive control. Common miss: Assuming any task involving stimuli is mainly sensory rather than recognizing the executive demand in inhibiting an automatic response. This is correct. Inhibiting an automatic response is an executive-control demand. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.B: Phototransduction occurs in retinal photoreceptors and does not explain prefrontal activation during response inhibition.
distractor_rationales.C: Spinal reflex integration involves spinal circuits rather than higher-order cognitive control.
distractor_rationales.D: Auditory transduction occurs in the cochlea, not primarily in the prefrontal cortex.

items.stem: A public health researcher describes a socioeconomic gradient in health. Which pattern would best illustrate this concept?

choices.text: Each step down in income or education is associated with progressively worse average health outcomes.
Only the very poorest group differs from all other groups in health outcomes.
Health outcomes are unrelated to social position after childhood.
Social class affects cultural tastes but cannot affect health.

items.explanation: A socioeconomic gradient in health means health outcomes tend to vary progressively across levels of socioeconomic status, not only between the poorest group and everyone else. Common miss: Interpreting inequality in health as only a poverty-versus-nonpoverty contrast rather than a graded relationship. This is correct. The gradient is a stepwise relationship across the social hierarchy. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.B: This describes a threshold difference, not a gradient across multiple levels.
distractor_rationales.C: The gradient concept specifically asserts that social position is related to health.
distractor_rationales.D: Social class can influence health through resources, exposure, stress, and access to care.

items.stem: A fictional individual hears voices when no external speaker is present and holds a fixed belief that coworkers are secretly broadcasting thoughts through office lights despite contrary evidence. These symptoms are most characteristic of:

choices.text: Psychosis-related symptoms
A specific phobia only
Normal sensory adaptation
Procedural learning

items.explanation: Hallucinations and delusions are psychosis-related symptoms. The stem is a fictional educational example and does not provide a clinical diagnosis. Common miss: Classifying unusual perceptual experiences as ordinary sensory phenomena rather than distinguishing hallucinations and delusions. This is correct. Hearing voices without an external source and holding fixed false beliefs are psychosis-related symptoms. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.B: Specific phobia involves marked fear of a specific object or situation, not hallucinations and delusions.
distractor_rationales.C: Sensory adaptation is reduced responsiveness to sustained stimulation, not perception without an external stimulus.
distractor_rationales.D: Procedural learning concerns skills and habits, not psychotic symptoms.

items.stem: In a psychophysics demonstration, a participant can just notice when 2 g are added to a 100 g weight. According to Weber's law, which added mass would the participant be most likely to just notice when lifting a 300 g weight?

choices.text: 2 g
4 g
6 g

items.explanation: Weber's law states that the just-noticeable difference is a constant proportion of the original stimulus intensity. If 2 g is just noticeable for 100 g, the Weber fraction is 2/100 = 0.02. For 300 g, 0.02 × 300 g = 6 g. Common miss: Assuming that the smallest detectable change is the same absolute amount at every stimulus intensity. This is correct. The just-noticeable difference scales proportionally with stimulus intensity. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.A: This treats the difference threshold as constant rather than proportional to the starting weight.
distractor_rationales.B: This increases the added mass but does not preserve the same Weber fraction.
distractor_rationales.D: This is much larger than the proportional difference implied by Weber's law.

items.stem: A student memorizes endocrine glands by imagining each gland placed at a specific stop along a familiar walk from home to school. During the exam, the student mentally walks the route to retrieve the list. Which memory strategy is being used?

choices.text: Method of loci
Maintenance rehearsal
State-dependent retrieval
Implicit priming

items.explanation: The method of loci involves linking information to familiar spatial locations and then mentally navigating those locations during retrieval. The route provides organized retrieval cues. Common miss: Classifying any study strategy as rehearsal instead of identifying the specific use of spatial retrieval cues. This is correct. The student uses a familiar spatial path as a structured memory aid. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.B: Maintenance rehearsal involves repeating information without necessarily adding meaningful spatial organization.
distractor_rationales.C: State-dependent retrieval involves improved recall when internal states match at encoding and retrieval, not spatial placement along a route.
distractor_rationales.D: Implicit priming involves prior exposure influencing later processing without deliberate retrieval.

items.stem: A researcher believes that people who drink tea are more patient. When reviewing interview transcripts, the researcher highlights comments from tea drinkers that sound patient but overlooks impatient comments from the same participants. Which cognitive bias is most clearly illustrated?

choices.text: The representativeness heuristic
Functional fixedness
Belief perseverance after disconfirmation only
Confirmation bias

items.explanation: Confirmation bias occurs when people preferentially seek, notice, or interpret evidence that supports an existing belief while discounting contrary evidence. The researcher selectively attends to transcript evidence that supports the hypothesis. Common miss: Mistaking biased interpretation of evidence for a general problem-solving limitation. This is correct. The researcher gives more weight to belief-consistent evidence. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.A: The representativeness heuristic involves judging category membership by similarity to a prototype.
distractor_rationales.B: Functional fixedness is difficulty using an object in a novel way, not biased evidence evaluation.
distractor_rationales.C: Belief perseverance refers to maintaining a belief after it has been discredited; the stem focuses on selective evidence processing.

items.stem: In a fictional educational vignette, a person experiences repeated intrusive thoughts about contamination and spends hours washing to reduce distress, despite recognizing that the behavior is excessive. This pattern is most characteristic of:

choices.text: Narcoleptic episodes
Dissociative amnesia
Antisocial personality traits
Obsessive-compulsive symptoms

items.explanation: Obsessions are intrusive, unwanted thoughts, and compulsions are repetitive behaviors performed to reduce distress. The vignette describes contamination obsessions and washing compulsions in a fictional educational context. Common miss: Focusing only on anxiety and missing the combination of intrusive thoughts and repetitive rituals. This is correct. Intrusive contamination thoughts and repetitive washing align with obsessive-compulsive symptoms. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.A: Narcoleptic episodes involve sleep-wake disruption, not intrusive thoughts and compulsive rituals.
distractor_rationales.B: Dissociative amnesia involves inability to recall important autobiographical information, not repetitive washing rituals.
distractor_rationales.C: Antisocial traits involve disregard for others' rights and norms, which is not described.

items.stem: During an acute startle response, adrenal medulla secretion rapidly increases circulating epinephrine and norepinephrine. This response is most closely associated with which pathway?

choices.text: Thyroxine suppression by the auditory cortex
Melatonin release from the pineal gland
Insulin release from pancreatic beta cells after a meal
Sympathetic-adrenal-medullary activation

items.explanation: Acute stress can activate the sympathetic nervous system and adrenal medulla, leading to rapid release of catecholamines such as epinephrine and norepinephrine. This supports immediate physiological arousal. Common miss: Confusing slower endocrine regulatory systems with the rapid catecholamine response to acute stress. This is correct. The adrenal medulla is part of the rapid sympathetic-adrenal-medullary stress response. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.A: The auditory cortex does not directly suppress thyroxine in the described pathway.
distractor_rationales.B: Melatonin is involved in circadian regulation and is not the rapid catecholamine response described.
distractor_rationales.C: Insulin regulates blood glucose after nutrient intake rather than mediating the startle response.

items.stem: A person whose parents worked hourly service jobs completes graduate training and enters a high-paying professional occupation. In sociology, this change is best described as:

choices.text: Upward intergenerational social mobility
Downward intragenerational social mobility
Horizontal mobility within the same class position
Role exit without class change

items.explanation: Intergenerational mobility compares social position across generations. Movement from parents' lower-status occupations to a higher-paying professional occupation is upward intergenerational mobility. Common miss: Confusing intergenerational mobility with mobility that occurs within one person's career. This is correct. The comparison is between generations and the direction is upward. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.B: Downward intragenerational mobility would refer to decline within the same person's lifetime.
distractor_rationales.C: Horizontal mobility involves changing roles or jobs without substantial class movement.
distractor_rationales.D: Role exit involves leaving a social role, not necessarily moving across class positions.

items.stem: A student is expected to attend a required evening laboratory session at the same time they are expected to care for a younger sibling at home. Which concept best describes the tension between these expectations?

choices.text: Anomie
Role strain
Status consistency
Role conflict

items.explanation: Role conflict occurs when expectations from different social roles are incompatible. The student role and family caregiver role impose conflicting demands at the same time. Common miss: Choosing role strain whenever a role is stressful, rather than identifying whether the conflict is within one role or between roles. This is correct. The tension is between two distinct roles. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.A: Anomie refers to normlessness or weakened social regulation, not incompatible role expectations.
distractor_rationales.B: Role strain occurs when demands within a single role are difficult to meet.
distractor_rationales.C: Status consistency refers to alignment among social status indicators, such as income and education.

items.stem: Damage to hair cells in the cochlea would most directly impair which process?

choices.text: Secretion of cortisol after social stress
Transduction of mechanical sound vibrations into neural signals
Encoding of autobiographical events in the hippocampus
Formation of class-based social networks

items.explanation: Cochlear hair cells convert mechanical vibrations caused by sound into neural signals sent through the auditory pathway. Damage to these cells can impair hearing. Common miss: Treating sensory receptors as passive structures rather than recognizing their role in transduction. This is correct. Cochlear hair cells are sensory receptors for auditory transduction. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.A: Cortisol secretion involves endocrine stress pathways rather than cochlear receptors.
distractor_rationales.C: Autobiographical event encoding involves memory systems, not cochlear hair cells.
distractor_rationales.D: Class-based social networks are sociological phenomena rather than sensory transduction processes.

items.stem: A participant hears a 20-word list once and immediately recalls mostly the first few and last few words. Which pattern is being demonstrated?

choices.text: Habituation
Opponent-process theory
Fundamental attribution error
Serial position effect

items.explanation: The serial position effect refers to better recall of items at the beginning and end of a list. The beginning reflects a primacy component, and the end reflects a recency component. Common miss: Labeling any memory advantage as priming instead of recognizing the position-based recall pattern. This is correct. The recall pattern favors early and late list items. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.A: Habituation is decreased response to repeated stimulation.
distractor_rationales.B: Opponent-process theory explains aspects of color vision and some motivational states, not list-position memory patterns.
distractor_rationales.C: Fundamental attribution error concerns explaining others' behavior by dispositions rather than situations.

items.stem: During a problem-solving task, a participant cannot think to use a binder clip as a temporary zipper pull because they think of it only as a device for holding papers together. This difficulty best illustrates:

choices.text: Out-group homogeneity
Divided attention
Sensory accommodation
Functional fixedness

items.explanation: Functional fixedness is a cognitive bias that limits problem solving by making it difficult to see objects as having uses beyond their typical functions. Common miss: Confusing a barrier to creative use of objects with a limitation in sensory attention. This is correct. The participant is constrained by the object's usual function. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.A: Out-group homogeneity involves perceiving members of another group as more similar to one another.
distractor_rationales.B: Divided attention concerns processing multiple tasks or stimuli at once, not generating alternate object uses.
distractor_rationales.C: Sensory accommodation is not the relevant problem-solving concept here.

items.stem: A person remembers reading a surprising fact but later incorrectly claims that a close friend told it to them. Which memory error is most directly illustrated?

choices.text: Formal operational thought
Sensory adaptation
Source monitoring error
Negative reinforcement

items.explanation: Source monitoring involves identifying where a memory came from. Misattributing a fact learned from reading to a conversation with a friend is a source monitoring error. Common miss: Treating every memory error as forgetting rather than distinguishing content retrieval from source attribution. This is correct. The content is remembered, but the source is misidentified. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.A: Formal operational thought involves abstract reasoning, not source attribution.
distractor_rationales.B: Sensory adaptation is reduced responsiveness after sustained stimulation.
distractor_rationales.D: Negative reinforcement strengthens behavior by removing an aversive stimulus.

items.stem: In a fictional animal-learning study, animals first experience unavoidable mild stressors. Later, when escape becomes possible, many do not attempt to escape. This pattern is most consistent with:

choices.text: Observational modeling
Stimulus discrimination
Learned helplessness
Latent learning in a maze

items.explanation: Learned helplessness can occur when exposure to uncontrollable aversive events leads an organism to stop trying to avoid or escape even when control becomes possible. Common miss: Assuming that failure to act reflects lack of ability rather than a learned expectation of uncontrollability. This is correct. Prior uncontrollability reduces later escape attempts. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.A: Observational modeling involves learning by watching another individual.
distractor_rationales.B: Stimulus discrimination involves responding differently to distinct cues.
distractor_rationales.D: Latent learning refers to learning that is not immediately expressed until motivation or reinforcement changes.

items.stem: A sociologist argues that what counts as a normal transition to adulthood differs across cultures and historical periods because societies assign different meanings to work, marriage, education, and independence. This argument most closely reflects:

choices.text: Punishment generalization
Vestibular transduction
Fixed action pattern theory only
Social constructionism

items.explanation: Social constructionism emphasizes that categories and meanings are created and maintained through social processes. The idea that adulthood is defined differently across cultures and time periods fits this perspective. Common miss: Assuming age categories are purely biological and overlooking socially assigned meanings. This is correct. The concept of adulthood is treated as socially defined rather than purely biological. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.A: Punishment generalization is not the concept described.
distractor_rationales.B: Vestibular transduction concerns balance and motion sensation.
distractor_rationales.C: Fixed action patterns are innate behavioral sequences and do not explain culturally variable meanings.

items.stem: A neuroscience study finds that unexpected rewards produce increased firing in midbrain neurons that project to the nucleus accumbens. Which neurotransmitter system is most strongly implicated?

choices.text: Oxytocin only
Melatonin
Histamine only
Dopamine

items.explanation: Dopaminergic pathways from the midbrain to reward-related regions such as the nucleus accumbens are strongly involved in reward prediction and reinforcement learning. Common miss: Associating reward with any hormone or neurotransmitter rather than identifying the mesolimbic dopamine pathway. This is correct. The mesolimbic dopamine system is central to reward processing. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.A: Oxytocin is associated with social bonding and other functions but is not the main midbrain-to-nucleus accumbens reward signal described.
distractor_rationales.B: Melatonin is primarily associated with circadian rhythms.
distractor_rationales.C: Histamine has roles in arousal and immune responses but is not the primary reward-prediction system described.

items.stem: A student who is overwhelmed by multiple deadlines creates a schedule, asks for one deadline extension, and divides the work into smaller tasks. This coping response is best classified as:

choices.text: Classical conditioning
Emotion-focused coping only
Problem-focused coping
Identity diffusion

items.explanation: Problem-focused coping attempts to change the stressor or one's practical relationship to it. Scheduling, requesting an extension, and breaking tasks into parts directly address the demands. Common miss: Classifying any stress-management behavior as emotion-focused without asking whether it changes the stressor. This is correct. The student is taking actions to manage the source of stress. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.A: Classical conditioning involves associating stimuli, not planning around deadlines.
distractor_rationales.B: Emotion-focused coping regulates emotional distress; the stem emphasizes practical changes to the stressor.
distractor_rationales.D: Identity diffusion involves lack of exploration and commitment, not coping with deadlines.

items.stem: A person judges depth partly because each eye receives a slightly different image of the same object. This depth cue is called:

choices.text: Weber fraction
Retinal disparity
Olfactory adaptation
Auditory shadowing

items.explanation: Retinal disparity is a binocular depth cue created by the slightly different images projected onto the two retinas. The visual system uses this difference to infer depth. Common miss: Confusing binocular depth cues with general stimulus-detection principles. This is correct. It describes a binocular cue based on differences between the two retinal images. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.A: A Weber fraction concerns the proportional change needed to detect a stimulus difference.
distractor_rationales.C: Olfactory adaptation concerns reduced smell sensitivity after sustained odor exposure.
distractor_rationales.D: Auditory shadowing is an attention task involving repeated speech input, not binocular depth perception.

items.stem: A person solving a logic puzzle tests every possible arrangement systematically until one satisfies all constraints. This strategy is best described as:

choices.text: Social facilitation
A heuristic
Sensitization
An algorithm

items.explanation: An algorithm is a systematic, step-by-step procedure that can guarantee a solution if applied correctly. Testing every possible arrangement is algorithmic problem solving. Common miss: Calling any problem-solving method a heuristic without considering whether the method is exhaustive and guaranteed. This is correct. The strategy is exhaustive and rule-based.
