Social identity formation

questions.explanation: A 2-back task requires participants to monitor incoming stimuli and compare each current item with one presented two steps earlier. This requires working memory maintenance and updating. Common miss: Treating any task involving remembered information as long-term memory rather than working memory. This is correct. The task requires active updating of recently presented information. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.A: Classical conditioning involves learned associations between stimuli, not tracking recent items in memory.
distractor_rationales.C: An absolute sensory threshold is the minimum detectable stimulus intensity, which the 2-back task does not assess.
distractor_rationales.D: Social identity formation concerns self-concept and group membership, not short-term cognitive updating.

questions.stem: Which design feature best supports a causal interpretation of the effect of sleep restriction on memory performance?

choices.text: Participants were randomly assigned to normal-sleep or restricted-sleep groups.
Participants completed both free-recall and cued-recall tests.
Participants studied neutral word pairs.
Participants rated their motivation after the study.

questions.explanation: Random assignment helps distribute potential confounds across groups, strengthening causal inference about sleep restriction. Multiple outcome measures and neutral stimuli may improve measurement, but they do not support causality as directly. Common miss: Choosing a useful measurement feature rather than the feature that most directly supports causal inference. This is correct. Random assignment is the strongest listed feature for causal inference. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.B: Using two memory tests provides more information about retrieval but does not by itself establish causality.
distractor_rationales.C: Neutral word pairs may control emotional content but do not eliminate group differences without random assignment.
distractor_rationales.D: Motivation ratings help evaluate a possible alternative explanation but do not create equivalent groups.

questions.stem: Which alternative explanation for the memory findings is most directly weakened by Table 2?

choices.text: The restricted-sleep group was much less motivated than the normal-sleep group.
The restricted-sleep group experienced greater fatigue than the normal-sleep group.
The cued-recall test provided retrieval cues.
The sleep manipulation affected working memory.

questions.explanation: Motivation ratings were similar across groups: 5.8 in the normal-sleep group and 5.6 in the restricted-sleep group. This weakens the claim that lower performance was primarily due to substantially lower motivation in the restricted-sleep group. Common miss: Assuming any self-report difference is a confound instead of checking the direction and size of the reported values. This is correct. The motivation scores are nearly the same, so motivation differences are unlikely to fully explain the performance gap. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.B: Table 2 supports, rather than weakens, greater fatigue in the restricted-sleep group.
distractor_rationales.C: The existence of retrieval cues is part of the task structure, not an alternative explanation weakened by motivation and fatigue data.
distractor_rationales.D: The 2-back results are consistent with an effect on working memory, not weakened by Table 2.

questions.stem: Based on Table 1, what is the approximate difference in 2-back accuracy between the normal-sleep and restricted-sleep groups?

choices.text: 4 percentage points
7 percentage points
14 percentage points
20 percentage points

questions.explanation: The normal-sleep group had 87% accuracy and the restricted-sleep group had 73% accuracy. The difference is 87 minus 73, or 14 percentage points. Common miss: Mixing the word-recall columns with the percentage-accuracy column. This is correct. The 2-back accuracy difference is 14 percentage points. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.A: This is closer to the difference in free recall means than to the 2-back accuracy difference.
distractor_rationales.B: This underestimates the 2-back difference.
distractor_rationales.D: This is larger than the observed accuracy difference.

passages.title: Neighborhood Resources and Stress Physiology
passages.body:
A community psychology team studied 120 adults living in three neighborhoods that differed in access to public transportation, grocery stores, and safe recreational spaces. Participants completed a perceived-stress scale, provided a morning saliva sample for cortisol measurement, and reported how often they used neighborhood recreational spaces. The investigators did not randomly assign participants to neighborhoods. They collected age, income, and employment status to use as covariates in later analyses.

Neighborhood characteristics and participant outcomes
Neighborhood resource level | Mean monthly household income | Mean perceived stress score | Mean morning cortisol, nmol/L | Mean recreational-space use, days/week
High | $5200 | 13.1 | 11.2 | 3.8
Moderate | $3900 | 17.4 | 13.9 | 2.1
Low | $2600 | 22.0 | 16.7 | 0.8

Conceptual model — The researchers hypothesized that neighborhood resource access may influence stress partly through daily opportunities for exercise, social interaction, and perceived control.

questions.stem: Which conclusion is most justified by the data in Table 1?

choices.text: Income is unrelated to neighborhood resource level.
Neighborhood resource level causes cortisol changes independently of income.
Recreational-space use has no relationship to stress.
Lower neighborhood resource level is associated with higher perceived stress and higher morning cortisol.

questions.explanation: The table shows that as neighborhood resource level decreases from high to low, perceived stress rises from 13.1 to 22.0 and morning cortisol rises from 11.2 to 16.7 nmol/L. Because participants were not randomly assigned to neighborhoods, a causal conclusion is not warranted from these data alone. Common miss: Interpreting an observational gradient as proof of independent causation. This is correct. The table supports an association between resource level and both stress indicators. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.A: Mean income differs across resource levels, so this statement is contradicted by the table.
distractor_rationales.B: The observational design and income differences prevent a strong independent causal conclusion.
distractor_rationales.C: Recreational-space use varies with resource level in a direction consistent with stress differences; the table does not show no relationship.

questions.stem: The investigators included income and employment status as covariates primarily because these variables could:

choices.text: Guarantee that the study becomes a randomized experiment.
Act as confounders related to both neighborhood resources and stress outcomes.
Eliminate the need for measuring cortisol.
Convert perceived stress into an independent variable.

questions.explanation: Income and employment status may influence where people live and may also influence stress physiology and perceived stress. Including them as covariates helps evaluate whether the neighborhood association remains after accounting for these potential confounds. Common miss: Assuming covariate adjustment fully solves the limitations of nonrandomized research. This is correct. Covariates can help address plausible confounding in observational research. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.A: Statistical adjustment does not make a nonrandomized study equivalent to a randomized experiment.
distractor_rationales.C: Cortisol remains a separate physiological outcome measure even if covariates are included.
distractor_rationales.D: Perceived stress remains an outcome measure in the described analysis.

questions.stem: Which sociological perspective would most likely emphasize that unequal neighborhood resources reflect competition over scarce material advantages and contribute to health inequality?

choices.text: Conflict theory
Symbolic interactionism
Exchange-ratio psychophysics
Information-processing theory

questions.explanation: Conflict theory emphasizes power, inequality, and competition over resources. The passage concerns unequal neighborhood resources and stress-related health indicators, making conflict theory the best match. Common miss: Choosing symbolic interactionism because the topic involves perceptions, while the stem asks about structural inequality and resource competition. This is correct. Conflict theory focuses on inequality and resource distribution. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.B: Symbolic interactionism focuses more on meanings created through microlevel interactions, not primarily on structural competition over resources.
distractor_rationales.C: Psychophysics concerns sensory detection and perception, not sociological inequality.
distractor_rationales.D: Information-processing theory concerns cognition, not distribution of neighborhood resources.

questions.stem: The researchers hypothesize that recreational-space use partly explains the association between neighborhood resources and stress. In this hypothesis, recreational-space use is best described as a:

choices.text: Randomization procedure
Placebo
Dependent variable only
Mediator

questions.explanation: A mediator is a variable through which an independent variable may influence an outcome. The passage's conceptual model suggests neighborhood resources may affect stress partly by shaping opportunities for exercise, social interaction, and perceived control through recreational-space use. Common miss: Labeling every measured variable as a dependent variable instead of identifying its hypothesized role in a causal pathway. This is correct. Recreational-space use is proposed as part of the pathway linking resources to stress. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.A: Randomization is an assignment procedure, not a measured explanatory pathway.
distractor_rationales.B: A placebo is an inert treatment or condition used as a comparison, which is not described.
distractor_rationales.C: Recreational-space use is measured, but the hypothesis gives it a pathway role rather than treating it only as an endpoint.

questions.stem: Which study modification would best strengthen causal inference about whether increased access to recreational spaces reduces stress?

choices.text: Exclude cortisol measurements and rely only on self-reported neighborhood satisfaction.
Measure perceived stress once in a larger sample from the same three neighborhoods.
Randomly assign comparable neighborhoods to receive new recreational-space improvements at different times and measure stress before and after implementation.
Recruit only participants who already use recreational spaces daily.

questions.explanation: Randomly assigning comparable neighborhoods to receive improvements at different times creates a stronger quasi-experimental or experimental basis for causal inference, especially with pre-post measurement. The other options do not adequately address confounding or temporal order. Common miss: Assuming larger sample size alone converts an observational comparison into a causal design. This is correct. Random assignment and pre-post measurement strengthen causal inference. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.A: Removing physiological measurement would reduce measurement breadth and not improve causality.
distractor_rationales.B: A larger cross-sectional sample may improve precision but does not solve the causal limitation.
distractor_rationales.D: Recruiting only daily users restricts the sample and prevents evaluating changes in access for nonusers.

passages.title: Conditioning and Sound Sensitivity in a Virtual Environment
passages.body:
A behavioral science lab used a virtual environment to study how neutral sounds can acquire emotional significance. During acquisition, participants repeatedly heard Tone A immediately before an unpleasant but safe burst of white noise. Tone B was presented equally often but was never followed by the white noise. Skin conductance response was recorded as an index of autonomic arousal. In an extinction phase, both tones were presented without the white noise. In a final test, participants heard Tone C, which was acoustically similar to Tone A but slightly lower in pitch.

Mean skin conductance response in arbitrary units
Phase and stimulus | Mean response
Late acquisition: Tone A | 0.78
Late acquisition: Tone B | 0.22
Late extinction: Tone A | 0.31
Late extinction: Tone B | 0.20
Final test: Tone C | 0.49

Stimulus arrangement — Tone A and Tone C were similar in pitch, whereas Tone B was clearly distinct from both.

questions.stem: During acquisition, Tone A is best described as the:

choices.text: Unconditioned response
Conditioned stimulus
Negative reinforcer
Extinction stimulus

questions.explanation: Tone A was initially neutral but was repeatedly presented before an unpleasant burst of white noise. Through pairing, Tone A became a conditioned stimulus capable of producing increased autonomic arousal. Common miss: Labeling the unpleasant white noise and the predictive tone with the same conditioning term. This is correct. Tone A acquired predictive value through pairing with the white noise. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.A: The unconditioned response would be the natural arousal response to the unpleasant white noise, not Tone A.
distractor_rationales.C: A negative reinforcer strengthens behavior by removing an aversive stimulus; Tone A is a cue, not a removed consequence.
distractor_rationales.D: Extinction is a process in which the conditioned stimulus is presented without the unconditioned stimulus, not the label for Tone A during acquisition.

questions.stem: Which result in Table 1 provides the strongest evidence that conditioning occurred during acquisition?

choices.text: Tone B was presented equally often as Tone A.
Late extinction response to Tone B was 0.20.
Final test response to Tone C was lower than late acquisition response to Tone A.
Late acquisition response was higher to Tone A than to Tone B.

questions.explanation: Conditioning is shown by a larger response to the stimulus paired with the unpleasant white noise than to the unpaired control stimulus. Tone A produced a mean response of 0.78, compared with 0.22 for Tone B during late acquisition. Common miss: Choosing a procedural control rather than the response difference that demonstrates learning. This is correct. A higher response to the paired tone than the unpaired tone indicates learned association. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.A: Equal presentation frequency is a useful control, but it is a design feature rather than the observed evidence of conditioning.
distractor_rationales.B: A low response to Tone B during extinction does not by itself demonstrate acquisition.
distractor_rationales.C: This relates more to generalization and reduced responding after extinction than to acquisition itself.

questions.stem: The response to Tone C during the final test is most consistent with:

choices.text: Retroactive interference
Negative punishment
Conservation
Stimulus generalization

questions.explanation: Tone C was similar to Tone A and produced an elevated skin conductance response relative to Tone B. Responding to a stimulus similar to the conditioned stimulus is stimulus generalization. Common miss: Treating all reduced responses after acquisition as extinction, even when the question asks about responding to a similar new stimulus. This is correct. Tone C resembles Tone A and evokes a conditioned-like response. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.A: Retroactive interference concerns new learning impairing old memory, not generalization of conditioned responses.
distractor_rationales.B: Negative punishment involves removing a desirable consequence to reduce behavior, not responding to a similar sensory cue.
distractor_rationales.C: Conservation is a cognitive-developmental concept unrelated to conditioned arousal.

questions.stem: Which physiological system is most directly reflected by skin conductance responses in this study?

choices.text: Photoreceptor adaptation
Voluntary skeletal muscle contraction
Long-term declarative memory storage only
Autonomic nervous system arousal

questions.explanation: Skin conductance is commonly used as an index of autonomic arousal because sweat gland activity changes electrical conductance at the skin. It is not primarily a measure of voluntary movement or visual receptor adaptation. Common miss: Treating any physiological measure as a direct measure of conscious memory rather than identifying the relevant autonomic process. This is correct. Skin conductance reflects autonomic arousal, especially sympathetic activity. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.A: Photoreceptor adaptation occurs in the visual system and is unrelated to the skin conductance measure.
distractor_rationales.B: Skeletal muscle contraction is measured more directly by motor behavior or electromyography, not skin conductance.
distractor_rationales.C: Declarative memory storage is not directly measured by skin conductance.

questions.stem: Why was Tone B important to the design of the study?

choices.text: It served as an unpaired comparison stimulus to help show that elevated responding was specific to Tone A.
It served as the unpleasant unconditioned stimulus.
It guaranteed that extinction could not occur.
It removed the need to measure skin conductance.

questions.explanation: Tone B was presented equally often but was never followed by the unpleasant noise. This makes it a useful control stimulus, helping distinguish learning specific to the Tone A-noise pairing from general reactivity to any tone. Common miss: Overlooking the importance of a control stimulus in distinguishing specific conditioning from general arousal. This is correct. Tone B controls for responses to tones that are not paired with the aversive event. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.B: The unpleasant burst of white noise, not Tone B, served as the unconditioned stimulus.
distractor_rationales.C: Tone B does not prevent extinction; extinction occurs when conditioned cues are presented without the unconditioned stimulus.
distractor_rationales.D: Tone B is part of the stimulus design, but physiological measurement is still needed to assess response.

passages.title: Identity, Group Membership, and Academic Feedback
passages.body:
A developmental psychology research group examined how social identity salience affects interpretation of academic feedback. High school students completed a difficult reasoning task and then received standardized written feedback stating that their score was below the sample average. Before receiving feedback, students were randomly assigned to one of two writing prompts. In the personal-values condition, students wrote about an important personal value. In the group-comparison condition, students wrote about ways their school group was viewed by students from a nearby school. After feedback, students rated perceived threat, expected future performance, and willingness to attempt a similar task.

Mean post-feedback ratings on 1 to 7 scales
Condition | Perceived threat | Expected future performance | Willingness to attempt similar task
Personal-values prompt | 3.0 | 4.9 | 5.5
Group-comparison prompt | 4.8 | 3.8 | 4.1

Interpretive note — All participants received identical task instructions and identical feedback; only the pre-feedback writing prompt differed across conditions.

questions.stem: Which feature of the study most supports the claim that differences in post-feedback ratings were caused by the writing prompt manipulation?

choices.text: Students completed a difficult reasoning task.
Students were randomly assigned to the writing prompt conditions.
Students attended high school.
Students rated willingness on a 1 to 7 scale.

questions.explanation: Random assignment helps make the groups comparable before the manipulation, supporting a causal interpretation of differences after feedback. The other features describe the task, sample, or measurement scale but do not support causality as directly. Common miss: Confusing an outcome measurement method with a design feature that supports causal inference. This is correct. Random assignment is the key causal design feature. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.A: The difficult task helps create a feedback situation but does not control preexisting group differences.
distractor_rationales.C: The sample describes who participated, not whether the prompt caused rating differences.
distractor_rationales.D: A rating scale measures an outcome but does not establish causality.

questions.stem: Based on Table 1, which statement best describes the effect of the group-comparison prompt relative to the personal-values prompt?

choices.text: It was associated with higher perceived threat and lower willingness to attempt a similar task.
It was associated with lower perceived threat and higher expected future performance.
It produced identical ratings across all outcomes.
It increased expected future performance more than willingness.

questions.explanation: The group-comparison prompt had higher perceived threat than the personal-values prompt, 4.8 versus 3.0, and lower willingness to attempt a similar task, 4.1 versus 5.5. It also had lower expected future performance. Common miss: Reversing which condition had higher threat after negative feedback. This is correct. It matches the observed direction of the ratings. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.B: This reverses the pattern shown in the table.
distractor_rationales.C: The ratings differ across conditions for all three outcomes.
distractor_rationales.D: Expected future performance was lower, not higher, in the group-comparison condition.

questions.stem: The group-comparison prompt most likely increased the salience of which aspect of self-concept?

choices.text: HPA-axis negative feedback
Sensory threshold
Procedural memory
Social identity

questions.explanation: Social identity refers to the portion of self-concept derived from group memberships. Writing about how one's school group is viewed by another school group makes group membership salient. Common miss: Treating any group-related prompt as merely stress-related without identifying the social identity manipulation. This is correct. The prompt explicitly concerns group membership and intergroup perception. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.A: HPA-axis feedback is a stress physiology mechanism, not the self-concept element manipulated by the prompt.
distractor_rationales.B: A sensory threshold concerns stimulus detection, not self-concept.
distractor_rationales.C: Procedural memory concerns learned skills and habits, not group-based self-definition.

questions.stem: Which interpretation would be most cautious and scientifically appropriate based on the passage?

choices.text: Personal-values writing eliminates all stress responses to academic feedback.
The group-comparison prompt permanently lowered students' academic ability.
The writing prompt changed students' immediate reactions to standardized negative feedback in this study.
Group identity has no effect on cognition or motivation.

questions.explanation: The study measured immediate ratings after a specific prompt and feedback manipulation. The data support differences in immediate reactions, not permanent changes in ability or complete elimination of stress. Common miss: Overgeneralizing short-term experimental results into permanent or universal claims. This is correct. It stays close to the design and measured outcomes. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.A: The personal-values condition had lower threat than the comparison condition but did not eliminate all stress.
distractor_rationales.B: The study measured expected performance, not actual permanent academic ability.
distractor_rationales.D: The passage data suggest group identity salience may affect perceived threat and motivation-related ratings.

questions.stem: A symbolic interactionist interpretation of the group-comparison condition would most likely emphasize that the feedback became more threatening because:

choices.text: Its meaning was interpreted through salient group labels and anticipated judgments from others.
The written feedback directly altered photoreceptor sensitivity.
The task removed all influence of social context.
The students had already achieved identity foreclosure.

questions.explanation: Symbolic interactionism emphasizes meanings formed through social interaction and interpretation. When group comparison is salient, identical feedback may be interpreted as more threatening because it is connected to group labels and expected evaluation by others. Common miss: Applying a broad biological or developmental label instead of using the theoretical perspective named in the stem. This is correct. It connects feedback meaning to social labels and perceived judgments. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.B: The prompt and feedback concern social interpretation, not sensory receptor sensitivity.
distractor_rationales.C: The group-comparison prompt increased, rather than removed, social context.
distractor_rationales.D: Identity foreclosure is commitment without exploration and is not measured or required by the passage.

passages.title: Multisensory Influences on Beverage Perception
passages.body:
A behavioral neuroscience lab examined whether ambient odors influence taste judgments. Seventy-two adults sampled the same unsweetened citrus beverage in three counterbalanced conditions: no ambient scent, a congruent lemon scent, and an incongruent coffee scent. Participants were not told that the scent condition changed across trials. After each sample, they rated perceived sweetness, perceived sourness, and purchase intention on 1 to 7 scales. In a separate adaptation task, participants detected faint lemon odors before and after continuous exposure to a moderate lemon scent for 3 minutes.

Mean ratings for identical beverage across ambient scent conditions
Condition | Perceived sweetness | Perceived sourness | Purchase intention
No ambient scent | 3.1 | 4.8 | 3.2
Congruent lemon scent | 4.2 | 4.5 | 4.5
Incongruent coffee scent | 2.7 | 5.0 | 2.8

Odor detection threshold in arbitrary concentration units
Time point | Mean lemon odor detection threshold
Before continuous odor exposure | 2.0
Immediately after 3 minutes of exposure | 6.0
Ten minutes after exposure ended | 3.0

Study design — Each participant experienced all beverage scent conditions in randomized order. The adaptation task was completed after the beverage ratings and used a detection threshold procedure for lemon odor.

questions.stem: Which conclusion is best supported by Table 1?

choices.text: Ambient scent influenced taste-related ratings even though the beverage was identical across conditions.
The coffee scent increased purchase intention more than the lemon scent.
Participants could not distinguish sweetness from sourness.
The no-scent condition produced the highest perceived sweetness.

questions.explanation: The passage states that the beverage was identical across conditions, yet ratings varied. The congruent lemon scent produced higher sweetness and purchase intention than the other conditions, supporting a multisensory influence on perception and choice. Common miss: Assuming that identical physical stimuli must produce identical perceptual ratings. This is correct. The same beverage received different ratings depending on ambient odor. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.B: The coffee scent produced lower purchase intention than the lemon scent.
distractor_rationales.C: The table shows separate sweetness and sourness ratings, but it does not show that participants could not distinguish them.
distractor_rationales.D: The congruent lemon scent produced the highest perceived sweetness.

questions.stem: The finding that odor context changed sweetness judgments most directly illustrates:

choices.text: Negative symptoms of psychosis
Operant extinction
Intergenerational mobility
Multisensory integration

questions.explanation: Multisensory integration occurs when information from different sensory modalities combines to shape perception. Here, smell influenced taste-related judgments of the same beverage. Common miss: Treating smell and taste as completely separate systems when perceptual judgments often combine multiple sensory inputs. This is correct. Olfactory context influenced gustatory perception. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.A: Negative symptoms of psychosis involve reductions in normal functioning, not odor-taste interaction.
distractor_rationales.B: Operant extinction concerns decreased behavior after reinforcement is removed, which is not the perceptual process tested.
distractor_rationales.C: Intergenerational mobility concerns class movement across generations and is unrelated to beverage perception.

questions.stem: The increase in lemon odor detection threshold immediately after continuous odor exposure in Table 2 is best explained by:

choices.text: Long-term potentiation
Sensory adaptation
Social loafing
Role conflict

questions.explanation: After continuous exposure to the lemon scent, participants needed a higher odor concentration to detect it. Reduced sensitivity after sustained stimulation is sensory adaptation. Common miss: Interpreting a higher detection threshold as improved sensitivity rather than reduced sensitivity. This is correct. Sustained exposure reduced sensitivity to that odor. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.A: Long-term potentiation is a neural mechanism related to synaptic strengthening, not the immediate threshold shift shown here.
distractor_rationales.C: Social loafing involves reduced individual effort in groups, not odor detection.
distractor_rationales.D: Role conflict involves incompatible demands from different social roles.

questions.stem: Why was counterbalancing the beverage scent conditions useful in this study?

choices.text: It guaranteed that participants could not experience sensory adaptation.
It made the beverage chemically different across scent conditions.
It removed the need for participant ratings.
It reduced the likelihood that condition order alone explained the rating differences.

questions.explanation: Counterbalancing distributes order effects across conditions. Because each participant experienced all scent conditions, counterbalancing helps prevent fatigue, practice, or carryover from being confounded with a specific scent condition. Common miss: Confusing counterbalancing with blinding or with changing the independent variable itself. This is correct. Counterbalancing addresses order as an alternative explanation. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.A: Counterbalancing reduces order confounds but does not make adaptation impossible.
distractor_rationales.B: The passage states that the same beverage was used across conditions.
distractor_rationales.C: Participant ratings were still needed as dependent measures.

questions.stem: Which additional procedure would best reduce demand characteristics in the beverage-rating portion of the study?

choices.text: Present only the congruent lemon scent condition to all participants.
Tell participants that lemon scent is expected to increase sweetness ratings.
Use a cover story that plausibly masks the purpose of the ambient scent manipulation.
Remove the no-scent comparison condition.

questions.explanation: Demand characteristics occur when participants infer the study hypothesis and alter behavior accordingly. A plausible cover story or masking procedure would reduce the chance that participants intentionally adjust ratings to match perceived expectations. Common miss: Assuming that participants' lack of explicit instruction about scent fully eliminates expectation effects. This is correct. Masking the study purpose can reduce hypothesis guessing. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.A: Using only one scent condition would eliminate key comparisons.
distractor_rationales.B: This would increase demand characteristics by revealing the expected effect.
distractor_rationales.D: Removing the no-scent condition would weaken the design by eliminating a baseline comparison.

passages.title: Stress Appraisal and Working Memory During Social Evaluation
passages.body:
Researchers studied how appraisal framing affects stress responses during a brief social-evaluation task. Ninety-six adults were randomly assigned to one of three groups. In the private-reading group, participants read a neutral passage alone. In the evaluative-threat group, participants gave a short speech while being observed and were told that poor performance would indicate weak communication ability. In the evaluative-challenge group, participants gave the same speech while being observed but were told that increased arousal could help them perform effectively. Participants completed a working-memory task afterward and provided saliva samples before and after the task.

Mean outcomes by task condition
Condition | Perceived control, 1 to 7 | Heart rate increase, beats/min | Salivary cortisol increase, nmol/L | Working-memory accuracy (%)
Private reading | 5.8 | 4 | 0.7 | 86
Evaluative threat | 2.7 | 18 | 4.6 | 71
Evaluative challenge | 4.9 | 16 | 2.6 | 79

Appraisal framing — The evaluative-threat and evaluative-challenge groups completed the same speech task; only the framing statement before the task differed.

questions.stem: Which interpretation is best supported by the data in Table 1?

choices.text: The private-reading group experienced the strongest stress response.
Challenge framing eliminated all physiological arousal during the speech task.
Challenge framing was associated with lower cortisol increase and better working-memory accuracy than threat framing during the same speech task.
Threat and challenge framing produced identical perceived control ratings.

questions.explanation: The challenge and threat groups completed the same speech task but differed in framing. Compared with threat framing, challenge framing showed lower cortisol increase, higher perceived control, and higher working-memory accuracy, while heart rate still increased substantially. Common miss: Assuming that lower cortisol means no arousal occurred, despite the heart-rate data. This is correct. The table supports a difference between challenge and threat framing on cortisol and working memory. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.A: The private-reading group had the lowest physiological changes.
distractor_rationales.B: The challenge group still showed a 16 beats/min heart rate increase and a cortisol increase.
distractor_rationales.D: Perceived control was higher in the challenge group than in the threat group.

questions.stem: The challenge framing most directly targeted participants' appraisal of:

choices.text: Whether social class is inherited genetically
Whether the speech sounds entered the cochlea
Whether the task used a fixed-ratio reinforcement schedule
Whether their resources could help them meet the task demands

questions.explanation: Stress appraisal involves evaluating a situation's demands and one's resources for coping with those demands. The challenge statement reframed arousal as potentially useful, increasing perceived control and resource appraisal. Common miss: Reducing stress appraisal to stimulus exposure alone rather than considering interpretation of demands and coping resources. This is correct. Challenge appraisal emphasizes the possibility that available resources can meet demands. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.A: The passage does not concern genetic inheritance of class.
distractor_rationales.B: The framing did not manipulate auditory transduction.
distractor_rationales.C: No reinforcement schedule was used in the speech task.

questions.stem: Which feature of the study most supports causal inference about the effect of appraisal framing?

choices.text: Heart rate was reported in beats per minute.
The private-reading task involved a neutral passage.
Working memory was measured after the task.
Participants were randomly assigned to the three groups.

questions.explanation: Random assignment helps distribute preexisting differences across conditions, strengthening the claim that differences in outcomes were caused by the task and framing manipulations. Common miss: Selecting a precise measurement detail rather than the design feature that reduces selection differences. This is correct. Random assignment is the key design feature for causal inference. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.A: Measurement units do not address causal inference.
distractor_rationales.B: A neutral reading task provides a comparison condition but does not by itself ensure equivalent groups.
distractor_rationales.C: Post-task measurement establishes timing but does not control selection differences as directly as random assignment.

questions.stem: Which result would most directly support the idea that reduced perceived control helped explain the working-memory impairment in the evaluative-threat group?

choices.text: The speech task lasts the same number of minutes in both evaluative groups.
The private-reading group has the smallest heart rate increase.
All participants report that they understood the instructions.
Across participants, lower perceived control statistically predicts lower working-memory accuracy even after accounting for task condition.

questions.explanation: If perceived control is part of the pathway linking threat framing to working-memory performance, then lower control should be associated with lower accuracy even when task condition is considered. This would support, though not prove by itself, a mediating role for perceived control. Common miss: Choosing a procedural similarity instead of evidence connecting the proposed mediator to the outcome. This is correct. It directly links the proposed psychological mediator to the cognitive outcome. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.A: Equal task duration is a procedural control but not evidence for the proposed mediator.
distractor_rationales.B: This describes a physiological difference for the comparison group but does not test perceived control as an explanatory pathway.
distractor_rationales.C: Instruction comprehension is useful but does not connect control appraisal to working memory.

questions.stem: Based on Table 1, what is the approximate difference in working-memory accuracy between the evaluative-challenge and evaluative-threat groups?

choices.text: 2 percentage points
8 percentage points
15 percentage points
18 percentage points

questions.explanation: The evaluative-challenge group had 79% working-memory accuracy, and the evaluative-threat group had 71% accuracy. The difference is 79 minus 71, or 8 percentage points. Common miss: Using the wrong column or comparing the threat group with private reading instead of challenge framing. This is correct. The working-memory accuracy difference is 8 percentage points. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.A: This is closer to the heart-rate difference between the two evaluative groups, not the accuracy difference.
distractor_rationales.C: This is the difference between private reading and threat accuracy, not challenge and threat accuracy.
distractor_rationales.D: This is the heart-rate increase in the threat group, not an accuracy difference.

passages.title: Adult Education Centers and Health Information Navigation
passages.body:
A community research team evaluated a short workshop designed to improve adults' ability to interpret online health information. The workshop taught participants how to identify source credibility, distinguish testimonials from population-level evidence, and compare numerical risks. Participants attended one of three adult education centers located in districts that differed in occupational composition and average household income. Workshop attendance was optional, so participants were not randomly assigned to attend. All participants completed a health-information comprehension test at baseline and four weeks later.

Mean health-information comprehension scores out of 100
Center district | Baseline score | Four-week score among nonattendees | Four-week score among workshop attendees | Households with reliable broadband (%) | Mean schedule predictability, 1 to 7
Working-class district | 58 | 60 | 72 | 62 | 2.1
Mixed-income district | 64 | 65 | 75 | 78 | 3.5
Professional-class district | 75 | 76 | 82 | 94 | 5.4

Resource context — The researchers proposed that broadband access and predictable work schedules may influence the ability to practice health-information skills outside the workshop.

questions.stem: Which limitation most directly affects causal claims about the workshop's effect on comprehension?

choices.text: The study included more than one education center.
The comprehension test was scored out of 100.
Participants chose whether to attend the workshop.
The researchers measured broadband access.

questions.explanation: Because attendance was optional, attendees may have differed from nonattendees in motivation, time availability, baseline skills, or access to resources. This selection issue limits causal inference. Common miss: Treating a clear score scale as a methodological weakness while missing self-selection into the intervention. This is correct. Self-selection into attendance creates a plausible confound. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.A: Including multiple centers can improve external relevance and does not itself weaken causality.
distractor_rationales.B: A 100-point scale is a measurement format, not the key causal limitation.
distractor_rationales.D: Measuring broadband access provides contextual information and does not create the main causal limitation.

questions.stem: The differences in reliable broadband access across districts most directly relate to which concept?

choices.text: Digital divide
Binocular disparity
Spontaneous recovery
State-dependent memory

questions.explanation: The digital divide refers to unequal access to digital technologies and internet resources. The table shows lower reliable broadband access in the working-class district than in the professional-class district. Common miss: Viewing internet access as a purely individual preference rather than a stratified resource. This is correct. Broadband inequality is a digital divide issue. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.B: Binocular disparity is a depth cue based on slightly different retinal images.
distractor_rationales.C: Spontaneous recovery is reappearance of a conditioned response after a rest period.
distractor_rationales.D: State-dependent memory concerns matching internal states at encoding and retrieval.

questions.stem: Which interpretation of the workshop is most consistent with functionalism?

choices.text: The workshop matters only because all health categories are meaningless.
The workshop helps an institution teach skills that support informed participation in social systems.
The workshop proves that class resources have no effect on learning.
The workshop is unrelated to any social institution.

questions.explanation: Functionalism emphasizes how social institutions contribute to social stability and functioning. An adult education center teaching health-information skills can be interpreted as helping individuals participate effectively in health and civic systems. Common miss: Equating all sociological analysis of institutions with inequality critique rather than matching the functionalist emphasis on social functions. This is correct. It frames the institution as serving a social function. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.A: Functionalism does not claim that categories are meaningless.
distractor_rationales.C: The passage shows resource differences across districts, so this claim is not supported.
distractor_rationales.D: Adult education centers are social institutions, and the workshop is institutional activity.

questions.stem: Based on Table 1, what is the difference between four-week scores for workshop attendees in the professional-class district and workshop attendees in the working-class district?

choices.text: 7 points
10 points
14 points
22 points

questions.explanation: Workshop attendees in the professional-class district scored 82, and attendees in the working-class district scored 72. The difference is 82 minus 72, or 10 points. Common miss: Calculating an improvement within one district when the question asks for a difference between two districts among attendees. This is correct. The score gap is 10 points. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.A: This is the difference between mixed-income and professional-class attendee scores, not working-class and professional-class attendee scores.
distractor_rationales.C: This is the improvement among working-class workshop attendees from baseline to follow-up, not the cross-district attendee gap.
distractor_rationales.D: This is the difference between professional-class attendees and working-class nonattendees.

passages.title: Recycling Behavior and Reinforcement Schedules in Dormitory Kitchens
passages.body:
A campus sustainability team tested behavioral strategies for improving recycling accuracy in dormitory kitchens. Twenty dormitory floors were randomly assigned to one of four conditions: informational signs only, a fixed-ratio points program in which floors earned a reward after every fifth correctly sorted item, a variable-ratio points program in which floors earned rewards unpredictably after an average of five correctly sorted items, or an observational-modeling condition in which residents watched a peer demonstrate correct sorting before signs were posted. In the reward conditions, a green light on the sorting station indicated that the sensor was active and points could be earned; a red light indicated that the sensor was off. After four weeks, point rewards were removed for one week while signs remained.

Mean percentage of items correctly sorted
Condition | Baseline week | Week 4 | Reward-removal week
Informational signs only | 43 | 55 | 52
Fixed-ratio points | 42 | 68 | 50
Variable-ratio points | 44 | 75 | 63
Observational modeling plus signs | 41 | 70 | 66

Assignment unit — The dormitory floor, rather than the individual resident, was the unit of assignment because rewards and signs were shared within floor kitchens.

questions.stem: In the reward conditions, the green light indicating that points could be earned is best described as a:

choices.text: Discriminative stimulus
Unconditioned response
Negative punisher
Sensory receptor

questions.explanation: A discriminative stimulus signals that a particular response is likely to be reinforced. The green light indicated that correct sorting could earn points. Common miss: Calling the cue a reinforcer rather than recognizing that it signals when reinforcement is available. This is correct. The light signaled the availability of reinforcement for correct sorting. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.B: An unconditioned response is an automatic response to an unconditioned stimulus, not a signal for reward availability.
distractor_rationales.C: A negative punisher removes a desirable stimulus to reduce behavior; the green light did not function that way.
distractor_rationales.D: A sensory receptor detects physical stimuli; the light itself is not a receptor.

questions.stem: The difference between the fixed-ratio and variable-ratio reward-removal results is most consistent with which principle?

choices.text: Reinforcement schedules affect only reflexes, not voluntary behavior.
Predictable rewards always produce greater persistence than unpredictable rewards.
Behavior reinforced on variable schedules is often more resistant to extinction than behavior reinforced on predictable schedules.
Removing rewards always increases the reinforced behavior.

questions.explanation: The variable-ratio condition declined less after reward removal than the fixed-ratio condition. Variable schedules can produce persistent responding because the absence of immediate reward is less clearly informative that reinforcement has ended. Common miss: Assuming predictable reinforcement always creates the strongest long-term behavior. This is correct. The table shows greater persistence after a variable-ratio schedule. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.A: Operant reinforcement schedules can affect voluntary behavior such as recycling choices.
distractor_rationales.B: The table shows the opposite pattern during reward removal.
distractor_rationales.D: Removing rewards usually decreases reinforced behavior, although the degree of decrease can vary.

questions.stem: In this study, the primary dependent variable was:

choices.text: The presence of dormitory kitchens
Assignment to reinforcement condition
Percentage of items correctly sorted
The number of possible answer choices on a survey

questions.explanation: The dependent variable is the measured outcome. The table reports recycling accuracy as the percentage of items correctly sorted across time and conditions. Common miss: Confusing the manipulated condition with the measured behavioral outcome. This is correct. Recycling accuracy is the outcome measured. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.A: Dormitory kitchens are part of the setting, not the measured behavioral outcome.
distractor_rationales.B: Condition assignment is an independent variable manipulated by the researchers.
distractor_rationales.D: The passage does not describe a survey-answer-choice measure as the primary outcome.

questions.stem: Because dormitory floors, not individual residents, were randomly assigned to conditions, which analytic concern is most important?

choices.text: Residents on the same floor may not provide statistically independent observations.
No baseline measure can be collected in a cluster design.
Random assignment is impossible when groups share kitchens.
The dependent variable must be a hormone measure.

questions.explanation: When groups rather than individuals are assigned, observations from individuals within the same group may be correlated because they share the same environment and intervention. Analyses should account for clustering or use the floor as the relevant unit. Common miss: Analyzing clustered data as if every individual observation were fully independent. This is correct. Shared floor conditions can create nonindependence among residents' behaviors. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.B: The study did collect baseline accuracy by condition.
distractor_rationales.C: Random assignment can occur at the group or cluster level.
distractor_rationales.D: The dependent variable can be behavioral, such as recycling accuracy.

passages.title: Mental Health Messaging, Stigma, and Help-Seeking Intentions
passages.body:
A campus research group tested how different messages influence responses to a fictional vignette about a student named R who has experienced repeated episodes of sudden intense fear, rapid heartbeat, trembling, and worry about having another episode. Participants were randomly assigned to read one of four messages before viewing the vignette: a neutral campus-services message, a biological-explanation message, a coping-continuum message emphasizing that distress varies in degree and can be managed with support, or a danger-focused message emphasizing rare extreme outcomes. Participants then rated recognition of clinically significant distress, stigma, and willingness to recommend help-seeking.

Mean outcomes by message condition
Message condition | Recognized clinically significant distress (%) | Stigma rating, 1 to 7 | Willingness to recommend help-seeking, 1 to 7
Neutral campus-services message | 62 | 3.8 | 3.9
Biological-explanation message | 76 | 3.5 | 4.4
Coping-continuum message | 72 | 2.7 | 5.1
Danger-focused message | 80 | 5.2 | 3.1

Ethical note — The researchers debriefed participants after the study and provided a list of campus and community support resources. The vignette was fictional and was not used to diagnose participants.

questions.stem: A labeling-theory interpretation of the danger-focused message would most likely emphasize that:

choices.text: Help-seeking ratings are unrelated to social meaning.
Panic-like symptoms are caused only by retinal processing.
Random assignment prevents all possible measurement error.
Applying stigmatizing labels can shape social reactions to the person described in the vignette.

questions.explanation: Labeling theory examines how labels and social reactions can influence identity, stigma, and treatment by others. The danger-focused message may increase stigmatizing interpretations of the vignette. Common miss: Treating labels as neutral descriptions rather than recognizing their possible social consequences. This is correct. It focuses on how labels affect social responses. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.A: Help-seeking attitudes can be strongly shaped by social meaning and stigma.
distractor_rationales.B: The vignette concerns psychological distress, not a retinal mechanism.
distractor_rationales.C: Random assignment improves causal inference but does not eliminate all measurement error.

questions.stem: The vignette's sudden episodes of intense fear, rapid heartbeat, trembling, and worry about having another episode are most consistent with symptoms commonly associated with:

choices.text: Specific learning disorder
Panic disorder
Dissociative fugue
A circadian rhythm sleep-wake disorder only

questions.stem: Which modification would best test whether message effects extend beyond intentions to actual behavior?

choices.text: Measure whether participants later click a resource link or attend an optional informational session.
Remove the vignette and ask only about favorite campus buildings.
Use only the message condition with the highest stigma rating.
Stop random assignment and allow participants to select their preferred message.

questions.explanation: Actual behavior can be assessed by observing a concrete action, such as clicking a resource link or attending a session. This would complement self-reported willingness ratings. Common miss: Assuming stated intentions are identical to later behavior without measuring an actual action. This is correct. It adds a behavioral outcome related to help-seeking. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractor_rationales.B: Favorite campus buildings would not measure mental-health help-seeking behavior.
distractor_rationales.C: Using only one condition would prevent comparing message effects.
distractor_rationales.D: Self-selection would weaken causal inference about message effects.
